reference.source: Williams Textbook of Endocrinology / Endocrine Society clinical practice guidance
clinicalPearls: Autosomal dominant form of primary aldosteronism caused by a chimeric CYP11B1/CYP11B2 gene, in which aldosterone synthase becomes regulated by adrenocorticotropic hormone (ACTH) rather than the renin-angiotensin system
Because aldosterone secretion is ACTH-driven, low-dose glucocorticoid (which suppresses ACTH) corrects the aldosterone excess, giving the alternative name glucocorticoid-remediable aldosteronism
It causes early-onset, often familial, hypertension that can be severe and treatment-resistant, with a high risk of early haemorrhagic stroke from intracranial aneurysms
Biochemistry shows a raised aldosterone-to-renin ratio with suppressed renin, and characteristically elevated hybrid steroids (18-oxocortisol and 18-hydroxycortisol)
Hypokalaemia is often milder or absent compared with other forms of primary aldosteronism, so normokalaemia does not exclude the diagnosis
Diagnosis is confirmed by genetic testing for the chimeric gene; management uses low-dose glucocorticoid to suppress ACTH and/or mineralocorticoid-receptor antagonists, avoiding over-suppression
reference.pathophysiology: Familial hyperaldosteronism type 1 arises from unequal crossing over between the highly homologous CYP11B1 (11-beta-hydroxylase) and CYP11B2 (aldosterone synthase) genes, creating a chimeric gene. This fusion places aldosterone synthase activity under the control of the ACTH-responsive CYP11B1 promoter, so aldosterone is produced ectopically in the ACTH-regulated zona fasciculata and is no longer governed by angiotensin II or potassium. The result is inappropriate, ACTH-dependent aldosterone excess causing sodium retention, volume expansion, renin suppression, and hypertension, together with production of the hybrid steroids 18-oxocortisol and 18-hydroxycortisol. Because ACTH drives the process, glucocorticoid suppression of ACTH reduces aldosterone.
additionalDifferentials: Familial hyperaldosteronism types II, III, and IV
Apparent mineralocorticoid excess and Liddle syndrome
additionalInvestigations: Plasma aldosterone-to-renin ratio with suppressed renin
Genetic testing for the chimeric CYP11B1/CYP11B2 gene (long-PCR or Southern blot)
Urine or plasma hybrid steroids 18-oxocortisol and 18-hydroxycortisol
Serum potassium and acid-base assessment (often only mild hypokalaemia)
Cerebral vascular imaging (e.g. MR angiography) to screen for intracranial aneurysms
Dexamethasone suppression demonstrating fall in aldosterone (supportive, historically used)
redFlags: Severe or resistant hypertension presenting in childhood or young adulthood
Family history of early haemorrhagic stroke or intracranial aneurysm
Marked hypokalaemia or its complications when present
Hypertensive end-organ damage at a young age
reference.prognosis: With early diagnosis and appropriate therapy blood pressure is usually well controlled and cardiovascular and cerebrovascular risk reduced, but undiagnosed disease carries a significant risk of early stroke from ruptured intracranial aneurysms and hypertensive complications. Aneurysm surveillance is advised in affected families.
pitfalls: Excluding primary aldosteronism because potassium is normal, when hypokalaemia is often mild in this condition
Over-treating with glucocorticoid and causing iatrogenic Cushingoid effects or growth suppression in children
Missing the familial nature and failing to screen relatives and assess for intracranial aneurysms
Relying on imaging for a nodule and overlooking a genetic, dexamethasone-suppressible cause
references: Endocrine Society clinical practice guideline on primary aldosteronism
management: Low-dose glucocorticoid such as dexamethasone or prednisolone to suppress ACTH and correct the aldosterone excess, titrated to avoid iatrogenic Cushingoid over-suppression
Mineralocorticoid-receptor antagonists such as spironolactone or eplerenone as an alternative or add-on to control blood pressure and potassium
Cerebral vascular imaging with MR angiography to screen for and monitor intracranial aneurysms given the high haemorrhagic stroke risk
Blood-pressure and electrolyte monitoring with cardiovascular end-organ surveillance
Careful glucocorticoid dosing in children to avoid growth suppression
Genetic counselling with testing for the chimeric CYP11B1/CYP11B2 gene and cascade family screening
